messages:
Marcus: Quick question — a customer is asking us for a single set of IPs they can allowlist on their corporate outbound proxy. They are doing strict hostname/SNI checks and also have an inline TLS intercepting proxy. What do we actually require?

Anya: Short answer: it depends on their proxy behavior. If the proxy allows TLS passthrough (SNI preserved) they can allowlist by hostname/SNI; if the proxy terminates TLS (MITM), hostname-based allowlisting won't work for us and they need to allowlist our egress IP ranges.

Marcus: They asked for a list of IPs — can we give a single static block for hosted API?

Anya: For hosted customers we don't have one global static IP block — edge nodes are regional and can rotate. We publish region-specific egress CIDRs per account for Dedicated/Private. For public hosted API we recommend hostname/SNI allowlist unless customer insists on IPs.

Sylvia: If they rely on the proxy to do TLS inspect, important gotcha: many proxies rewrite Host or strip SNI. In that case our routing may fail or they'll see cert errors. Ask them to verify the proxy preserves SNI or to configure a bypass for api traffic to known IPs.

Priya: Practical checklist to send the customer: 
- Allow outbound TCP 443 to api.redwood.ai (and related hostnames) OR allow our published CIDRs for their region.
- Ensure CONNECT method is allowed for HTTPS through the proxy (no HTTP-only rewrite).
- If proxy performs TLS interception, they must allowlist our IPs and not interfere with Host/SNI headers.
- Keep idle connection timeout >= 60s for streaming; shorter timeouts break long streaming responses.

Marcus: Can we give them a quick test they can run to confirm SNI passthrough?

Anya: Yes — openssl s_client is handy. Example: 
```
openssl s_client -connect api.redwood.ai:443 -servername api.redwood.ai
```
If the certificate shows our CN and the handshake includes SNI=api.redwood.ai, the proxy is not terminating TLS. If they see the proxy's cert, it's terminating.

Priya: Also a curl test behind the proxy: 
```
# use env proxy
curl -v --proxy http://proxy.corp:3128 https://api.redwood.ai/v1/models
```
Look for CONNECT and then the 200/401 from our API. If they get a 200 from the proxy's cert page or a replaced body, it's MITMing.

Sylvia: Note about ALPN/HTTP2 — our streaming path uses HTTP/2 by default. Some enterprise proxies downgrade or break h2. If they rely on proxy, ask them to allow ALPN h2 or keep a fallback for http/1.1. Streaming performance degrades badly if h2 is blocked.

Marcus: Any firewall port requirements?

Anya: Ports: outbound TCP 443 is required. Optionally 80 for redirects/healthchecks. If they want to whitelist IPs, give them the region CIDRs we provide in the account portal. For Dedicated/Private we can provide static egress IP buckets.

Priya: Another operational tip — if the customer uses a proxy that injects headers, proxies often add X-Forwarded-For. We can't rely on that for auth or routing. Also they should not rewrite Authorization/Date headers.

SRE-Bot: FYI: we ran a quick health-check from eu-west edge -> api traffic recently and IPs rotated across CIDR 34.120.0.0/14 and 35.190.0.0/16 in last 72h (example observation). Recommend telling customers rotation windows (~weekly) unless on Dedicated.

Marcus: Perfect. I'll send them a short blurb with the checklist and the openssl/curl tests. Anything to add for on-prem and air-gapped setups?

Anya: For on-prem/private: provide the private-only endpoints and static NAT config. They should set up outbound NAT rules that map to the static egress IPs we assign. Also ask them to allow our healthcheck user-agent string (we include it in the portal).

Sylvia: One last note — for streaming clients behind strict proxies: encourage customers to prefer a proxy bypass for long-lived client->server connections or increase idle timeouts. Chunked transfer and keepalives are fragile otherwise.

Marcus: Thanks team — I'll draft the reply and paste back here for review before sending to the customer. :thumbsup:
